text_html: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother because of a 4-day history of swelling of his face. Three weeks ago, he was treated with antibiotics for bronchitis, and his symptoms resolved. Height is at the 60th percentile, weight is at the 55th percentile, and BMI is at the 52nd percentile. Pulse is 92/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 104/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows periorbital edema bilaterally. Lungs are clear. Results of urine studies are shown: pH 5.6, blood negative, glucose negative, protein 4+, hyaline casts positive. If a biopsy specimen of this patient's kidney were obtained, it would most likely show which of the following findings?
explanation_html:
Educational Objective: Minimal change disease may present with findings such as dependent edema in the buttocks, lower back, and legs; foamy or dark-colored urine; hypoalbuminemia; and proteinuria. A biopsy of this patient's kidney is most likely to show fusion and effacement of the pedicels.

Evaluation: Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by edema secondary to excessive proteinuria resulting in hypoalbuminemia and diminished intravascular oncotic pressure.

Definition: Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and can be idiopathic or triggered by a recent infection or immune stimulus. Kidney biopsy exhibits pedicel effacement on electron microscopy.

Prevention: There is no known way to prevent minimal change disease.

Treatment: First-line treatment for minimal change disease includes high-dose corticosteroids. Other treatment options may include calcineurin inhibitors, rituximab, and cyclophosphamide.

Differential: This 8-year-old boy presents with periorbital edema as well as findings of proteinuria on urine studies after a recent infection. Fusion and effacement of pedicels on a kidney biopsy would be the most likely finding, as minimal change is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, E, and F.
